en: The Śatapañcāśatikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, one fascicle;
composed by Bodhisattva Deva and translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of North India during the Later Wei dynasty.
I now take refuge in the wise teacher, whose name is Deva and who possesses great wisdom;
he is able to expound the true Dharma through a hundred syllables, removing all false views and directing one toward the true nature of reality.
It is said:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
It is for the sake of destroying the view of a self (*ātman*) and [the notion] that all phenomena each possess their own distinct intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
The Sāṃkhya said:
"That all phenomena possess a single characteristic is my solemn vow.
For what reason and by what causal conditions is it established that all phenomena have a single characteristic?"
Because they all equally possess oneness, just as objects such as jars and garments each possess their own individual oneness;
for this reason, one should always know that all dharmas are termed "one-characteristic," and thus the meaning of oneness is established.
The internal [opponent] says: It is not one. Why? Because:
You have established a thesis asserting the meaning of "one" through a formal vow; is this one or two?
If it is one, there would be only the vow itself, and thus "one" could not exist.
For this reason, the "one" you have established is refuted.
The Vaiśeṣika says:
You assert "one," whereas I now establish "difference," because the fault of asserting "one" has been abandoned.
The internal [opponent] says:
If you establish "difference," I shall in turn establish "oneness.
Why is this? If you establish difference apart from causes, I likewise establish oneness apart from causes.
The Vaiśeṣika said:
"I wish to establish something distinct. Why is this so?"

Because all phenomena have distinct characteristics that differ from one another—just as the characteristics of elephants, camels, deer, horses, and other such species are each different—for this reason, the characteristics of all phenomena are distinct;
all phenomena are indeed different, and thus the principle of difference is established.
The internal [opponent] says:

If you claim that the meaning of "difference" is established because the characteristics of this and that are not identical, then because their characteristics are distinct, each phenomenon (*dharma*) is individually one.
Thus, the "difference" you have posited is undermined by its own essential statement.
Since it is essential to state that [the entity] is destroyed, one knows that the characteristic of difference cannot be established.
The opponent says:
Because the characteristics of identity and difference are not established, I now establish the characteristic of existence.
Because each phenomenon possesses its own characteristic, one should know that the meaning of "having characteristics" is established.
Because having characteristics is established, one should know that "identity and difference" are also established.
The internal [opponent] says:
If you now establish existence, there must necessarily be a cause for it.
If you establish existence without a cause, I likewise establish non-existence without a cause.
The opponent says:
I maintain that all phenomena (dharmas) exist. Why?

Because we perceive that each phenomenon possesses its own characteristic (lakṣaṇa). For example, like flowers in the sky, which cannot be apprehended because they lack substance and characteristics; whereas objects such as jars and garments do manifest practical utility. Therefore, one should know that all phenomena possess characteristics.
For this reason, the thesis is established.
The internal [opponent] says:
You assert that existence exists because it possesses the characteristic of existence.
Is it because of the absence of characteristics that existence occurs?
Both of these positions entail faults.

If the meaning of existence is established by means of manifest characteristics, then the manifest characteristic is existence and existence itself is also existence; thus, the two principles of existence cannot be established as distinct.
If one says that there is no cause, then one’s solemn vow is violated.
Since neither existence nor non-existence can serve as a cause, the [opponent's] position is refuted.
The opponent says:
If you refute my position of existence, you thereby establish non-existence;
once the principle of non-existence is established, existence can then be re-established.
It is like the food and drink of worldly people: it is because of prior coarseness and astringency that there is subsequently something delicious.
For this reason, when you refute my "existence," you should know that this [refutation] itself is non-existent.
The internal [opponent] says:
By what cause is your established "non-existence" accomplished?
"If you establish non-existence without a cause, I likewise establish existence without a cause.
The opponent asks:
"How is this known?"
Because they lack intrinsic nature and characteristics.
It is like a mirage in the heat, which itself lacks intrinsic nature and characteristics; how much less could even a small amount of water be found therein?
For this reason, not even a single atom’s worth of characteristic can be found in any phenomenon; therefore, my thesis that all things are without meaning is established.
The internal proponent says:
Is this "non-existence" you have established caused,
or is it uncaused?
If you say there is no cause, your solemn vow is empty;
if you say there is a cause, your solemn vow is undermined.
If you say there is neither [cause nor absence of cause], that too is not established.
The opponent says:
All phenomena have causes; therefore, your refutation of existence and non-existence is not tenable. Why is this so?
Just as there are mud, fibers, reeds, and rushes, one knows that all phenomena have causes.
The internal [opponent] says:
There are no causes.
You say that because there is a cause, there is existence; yet that which has a cause is non-existent.
If the clay, hemp, fibers, and so forth already existed within the clay [prior to the pot], they would not be causes. Why is this?
Because [the effect] already exists within the cause.
If it did not already exist within the cause, it would not qualify as a cause,
just as sand is not the cause of oil because there is no oil in the sand.
If one says that it both exists and does not exist, this meaning is likewise not established. Why?
Because there are two faults.
Furthermore, that which exists does not arise, nor does that which does not exist arise.
If things were to arise from no cause, what purpose would a cause serve?
If they were to arise from a cause, your solemn vow would be violated.
As for your previous statement that all phenomena arise from causes, this is not so.
The opponent says:
Since the functions of jars, garments, and so forth are currently perceived, one knows that all phenomena arise from causes; they do not come into being without depending on conditions.
The internal [proponent] says:
Your statement that "because there is an effect, there is a cause" does not establish this meaning. Why is this so?
Because they exist in relation to one another.
If you claim that the cause exists because the effect is seen to have utility, then the effect is also the cause.
If the effect is the cause, then there is no effect; since there is no effect, there is no cause. Therefore, both cause and effect are undermined.
If one says that [the self] arises from causes such as the mind, mastery, time, or space, then it is a causally conditioned phenomenon; being a conditioned phenomenon, it is impermanent.
If [things] exist through dependence on mastery, time, direction, and mutual form, they would not be established through causes.
The opponent says:
What I have stated is the truth.
The ancient seers of former times have declared thus: "This Dharma is definitive; it shall never be otherwise.
The internal [opponent] says:
Your statement that "it is so by nature" (dharmatā) is not a correct explanation.
As I have taught, my Dharma differs from yours.
That which exists within your Dharma does not exist within my Dharma;
that which exists within my Dharma does not exist within your Dharma.
Why is this? You claim that your doctrine is self-evident; if your doctrine were indeed so, it would merely be self-justifying.
To speak from a position of self-justification is devoid of rational coherence.
If there were no rational basis, then there would be nothing to be known.
If there is something to be known, one must further explain the superior cause.
To claim it is "thusness" (*dharmatā*) without a superior cause is irrational.
The outsider said:
"This is our school's doctrine.
The insider said:
The doctrine you speak of as your family tradition cannot be established.
Since your doctrine is not self-established, how can it establish other doctrines?
If it were to exist apart from causes, it would ultimately never be established.
From this point on, those who maintain such a doctrine do not accord with correct reasoning.
The opponent says:
There is no phenomenon that does not arise from causes, such as a rabbit’s horn, a tortoise’s hair, the son of a barren woman, or flowers in the sky.
Such non-existent dharmas can ultimately never be obtained.
Because they arise through causes and conditions—just as one seeks sesame seeds when pressing oil, or seeks clay when making a jar—a single dharma acting as a cause cannot produce multiple dharmas.
Furthermore, each thing has its own specific cause: for example, clay can produce a jar, but it is not the cause for a cloth;
threads can produce a cloth, but they are not the cause for a jar.
Seeking by this analogy, other phenomena are likewise so.
The internal [opponent] says:
As for your statement that "the cause can produce," the cause cannot produce.
Does this cause have something to be accomplished?
Is there something that is destroyed?
If the cause is something established, then you establish me as well as yourself.
If the cause is something destroyed, then I destroy myself as well as you.
By what analogy?
Just as fire can burn objects, it burns you and it burns me;
if it is hot in that place, it is likewise so here.
Furthermore, to clarify this meaning once more:
if one says that something is established by means of a cause, then what is established for you is also established for me.
Although there is that which arises from a cause, the cause and the dharma [the effect] are not established simultaneously.
You assert that the phenomenon of sound is permanent; state this with a solemn vow.
What is the reason? Its lack of physical form is the reason.
By what is it illustrated?
It is illustrated by space.
Space is formless and eternal; for this reason, sound is said to be eternal.
There is another explanation which states that sound is impermanent.
For what reason?
Because sound is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma), it is impermanent.
By what analogy?
It is like a jar, which is produced from clay, a wheel, a string, human effort, water, and so forth; because it arises through the cause of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), the jar is impermanent.
Likewise, sound arises from various conditions such as the lips, teeth, throat, and tongue; therefore, sound is also impermanent.
These two causes are incapable of establishing anything.
Your claim of "reality" may have its meaning established;
however, if you speak falsely with fallacious reasons, the principle will not stand.

In your statement regarding "essentiality" (*yāva*) and "vow" (*praṇidhāna*), when there is essentiality there is no vow, and when there is a vow there is no essentiality; since these two terms do not coexist, the concept of an "essential vow" (*yāva-praṇidhāna*) is undermined.
It is like how that which has not yet arisen cannot be a cause, and that which has already ceased is likewise not a cause.
Just as one who has not yet been born is not called "born," so too, that which has ceased is not "birth.
For this reason, there is no cause.
The opponent says:
"Although you refute cause and effect, because I maintain that there exists a self and its phenomena (ātma-dharma), cause and effect are thereby re-established.
The internal [opponent] says:
"When you say there exists a self and its phenomena, what constitutes their essence?"
If consciousness were the self, then consciousness would be impermanent; for the cognition of a jar ceases while the cognition of a cloth begins.
If consciousness were not the self, then the self would be devoid of cognition.
If I were devoid of cognition, there would be neither suffering nor pleasure.
Such a self, therefore, would lack any essential nature or characteristic.
If one says that I possess cognition because I am conjoined with cognition, then cognition itself—because it is conjoined with me—is likewise not cognition.
The opponent says:
There is a self. Why is this so?
[Opponent: Since objects such as jars and garments are "mine," one should know that there exists a self (*ātman*).
[Proponent:
This is incorrect, because it entails the fallacy of [the self] being identical with existence; for the jar would not be distinct from existence itself.
If there is "one-ness" that is not a jar, then "one-ness" existing apart from the jar should also be a jar; in that case, there would be many jars.
If "one-ness" is not a jar, then there is no jar at all.
The opponent says:
"There is a fault because [the pot] is one.
I now establish it as distinct, in order to abandon that fault of oneness."
The internal [opponent] says:
If you say they are different, then there is no jar; because it would both exist and not exist, there is no jar.
It is like saying that because a bhikṣu is different from a brāhmaṇa, one should know that there is neither a bhikṣu nor a brāhmaṇa.
If the pot were different from existence, it would be non-existent, just as a sword is seen to be distinct from its scabbard.
If the pot possessed both identity and difference, these too should be visible.
Since neither identity nor difference is perceived here, the thesis of difference is not established.
The opponent says:
Although unity and difference have been refuted, a jar is nonetheless perceived in the present.
It is like a flower in the sky; because it does not exist, it cannot be seen.
[Opponent: Since a jar is perceived through direct observation, one should know that the jar exists.
[Proponent:
No, it is not seen.
Why is it not seen?
When you say it is "seen directly," is it seen by the eye or is it seen by consciousness?
If it were the eye that sees, then a dead person, who also possesses eyes, should likewise see.
If it were consciousness that sees, then a blind person, who also possesses consciousness, should likewise see.
If neither the sense organ nor the consciousness sees individually, they will not see even when combined.
It is like a single blind person who cannot see; many blind people likewise cannot see.
The opponent says:
"Because there is color, there is a jar."
The internal [opponent] says:
You claim that because there is form (rūpa), there is a jar (ghaṭa).
Is this form and the jar one and the same, or are they different?
If the color were identical to the jar, then when one perceives another color, one should also perceive the jar.
If the color were distinct from the jar, then the jar would not be visible, and thus there would be no jar.
If one takes the perception itself to be the jar, then when the jar is in a concealed location and the eye does not see it, the jar should cease to be a jar.
If form were identical with the jar, then when the jar is destroyed, the remaining forms should also be destroyed.
The opponent says:
In my doctrine, dharmas are neither produced nor destroyed; thus, seeing is not destroyed, and non-seeing is also not destroyed.
Why is this? Because my Dharma is eternally present.
The effect exists within the cause; it is merely subtle and not manifest.
Because it exists beforehand, it subsequently attains completion.
For this reason, one knows that cause and effect exist.
The internal [opponent] says:
That which already exists need not be produced; it is like a jar that already exists in the clay, requiring no potter, or like cloth that already exists in the threads, requiring no weaver.
Since the jar and the cloth depend upon the labor of craftsmen for their completion, one knows that the effect does not exist within the cause.
If the effect already exists within the cause, then there would be no future phenomena.
If there were no future phenomena, then there would be no arising or ceasing.

Without arising and ceasing, there would be neither good nor evil; without good and evil, there would be no karma, transgressions, or the retribution of merit and demerit. In this way, all phenomena would be non-existent.
Furthermore, if the subtle fruit already exists within the cause while the coarse fruit does not, then this coarse fruit would be something previously non-existent that subsequently comes into being.
This constitutes arising and ceasing, which contradicts what you previously asserted.
Furthermore, if the subtle existed prior [to arising], it would not be a phenomenon subject to arising.
Because it would not be a phenomenon subject to arising, the three periods of time would be subverted.
If the three periods of time do not exist, one should know that all phenomena likewise do not exist.
If the effect already existed within the cause, then curd would already exist within milk.
If one says that it was previously non-existent and later comes to be, then one should know that it is a produced phenomenon.
For this reason, all phenomena must have existed beforehand within their causes; there is no further need for them to be produced.
The opponent says:

If it is a fault that the effect pre-exists within the cause, then we now assert that the effect arises after having previously not existed within the cause; thus, being free from the [extremes of] non-arising and cessation, there is no fault.
Because there is arising and cessation, it is both existent and non-existent.
The internal [opponent] says:
Non-arising and arising do not occur at the same time.
If the jar already existed within the clay, it would not require the wheel, the cord, human effort, and so forth, to be produced.
If it were non-existent like a tortoise’s hair, it could not be spun or woven to be of use.
For this reason, neither existence nor non-existence arises.
Furthermore, does the taking up of a body arise from itself or from another?
Both positions entail faults.
If it were produced by itself, what further need would there be for production?
For this reason, self-production has no substance.
If things do not arise from themselves, how could they arise from another?
To claim that they arise from both self and other is likewise subject to error.
For this reason, all phenomena are without arising.
The opponent says:
If there were no body, the three conditioned characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing would not exist.
If there are conditioned phenomena, then there must be unconditioned phenomena.
Since the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) are established, all phenomena (*dharma*) are also established.
The internal [opponent] says:
There are no conditioned phenomena.
Regarding your statement about the three characteristics: do they arise sequentially, or do they arise simultaneously?
There is a fault in both cases; there is a fault whether they arise sequentially or simultaneously.

If they were to arise sequentially, at the time of arising there would be neither abiding nor ceasing; at the time of abiding there would be neither arising nor ceasing; and at the time of ceasing there would be neither arising nor abiding.
For this reason, sequential arising is impossible.
Furthermore, if arising were to abide, then since arising itself lacks intrinsic nature, what would abide?
Since the essence of arising does not exist, how could abiding exist?
Without arising and without abiding, it is like the son of a barren woman; this is a non-existent thing.
If there were arising and abiding that could be extinguished by cessation, then since arising and abiding do not exist, how could cessation extinguish anything?
It would be like destroying a rabbit’s horn; there would be the empty name of "destruction" alone.
The opponent says:
You say that the sequence of arising, abiding, and ceasing cannot be apprehended; just as a second head or a third hand cannot be found, the three characteristics likewise cannot be apprehended.
If the three characteristics were simultaneous, they too could not be established. Why?
If cessation were present within arising, then that arising would not be true arising.
If there were arising within ceasing, then ceasing would not be ceasing.
The same refutation applies to the presence of arising and ceasing within abiding.

Since arising and ceasing are mutually contradictory, how could they exist at one and the same time? For this reason, the sequential arising of the three characteristics cannot be established, nor can their simultaneous arising be established.

Furthermore, as for your statement regarding the three characteristics: do they function as characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), or do they function as characteristics of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?

If they function as characteristics of the conditioned, then arising (*utpāda*), being itself conditioned, should possess three characteristics; the same would apply to duration (*sthiti*) and cessation (*nirodha*).

If such characteristics were thus infinite, then since the characteristics would be infinite, you should not say that conditioned phenomena possess only three characteristics; your solemn vow would then be violated.
If the characteristics themselves are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how can conditioned characteristics characterize the unconditioned?
The opponent says:
If you do not wish to allow them to function as conditioned characteristics, then they must function as unconditioned characteristics.
Why is this? Because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) pervades all places and has no spatial location; therefore, it should be characterized by the unconditioned.
The internal [opponent] says:
The unconditioned has no location.
I now ask you:
does space have a location?
Is it without location?
If space had a location, it would have to be at your side and also at his side.
If that were so, it would possess parts; and that which possesses parts must have boundaries.
If you say that space has no location or direction, does your body pervade space,
or does space pervade your body?
If space pervades your body and your body pervades space, then it would have boundaries, like a jar, a garment, or a folded cloth.
Because it has limits, it is impermanent; if space were likewise so, it too would be impermanent.
Furthermore, a permanent cause can produce a permanent effect.
If the cause is impermanent, how could the effect be permanent?
For example, as a jar arises from clay,
because the clay is impermanent, the jar is also impermanent.
Because it occupies a specific location, it is called impermanent.
Furthermore, regarding what you say about permanence: is it permanent because it has a cause, or is it permanent because it lacks a cause?
Both positions entail faults.
If you claim that what arises from causes is eternal, then things such as jars and garments, because they arise from causes, would likewise all be impermanent.
If you maintain that phenomena which do not arise from causes are eternal, I shall likewise maintain that phenomena which do not arise from causes are impermanent.
If there must be a phenomenon that arises from causes yet remains eternal, is this a statement consistent with reason,
or is it a partisan assertion?
You should now clearly explain its underlying cause once more.
The opponent says:
There are two kinds of causes:
the productive cause (kāraka-hetu) and the revealing cause (vyañjaka-hetu).
That which arises from a productive cause (*kāraka-hetu*) is impermanent, such as objects like jars or garments; because they arise from a productive cause, they are impermanent.

That which arises from a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*) is permanent, such as a lamp that can illuminate various objects in the dark; when the darkness departs and the objects appear, they are permanent because they are not produced things.
For this reason, that which arises from a producing cause (*kāraka-hetu*) is impermanent, while that which arises from a revealing cause (*vyañjaka-hetu*) is permanent.
The internal [proponent] says:
Objects such as jars exist because they are perceived through direct observation.
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is non-existent because it is not perceived through direct observation.
Why is this? Because the unconditioned lacks any essential nature or characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it is a non-entity (*dharma*).

By relinquishing both existence and non-existence, because both are abandoned, one is able to sever the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*), thereby attaining *nirvāṇa*.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"When, through the vision of the realm of wisdom, one sees that all phenomena are empty and consciousness has nothing to grasp, then the mind-consciousness ceases and the seeds cease."
The outsider said:
"If conditioned phenomena have no essential nature or characteristics, how can they possess reality?
The insider said:
It is like a dream.
All phenomena of conventional truth are like dreams; a dream is neither substantially existent, nor is it non-existent, nor does it arise without a cause.
Just as with the phenomena of conventional truth, they possess no marks of existence, no marks of non-existence, and do not arise without a cause.
It is like a house: if it possessed a substantial form (*svabhāva*), it should have been visible even before it was built;
yet if one says it does not exist [prior to construction], it could not be seen.
It is through the provisional assembly of beams, rafters, foundations, and walls that it comes to have functional utility; it is not without cause.
For this reason, all phenomena are neither existent, nor non-existent, nor are they without cause; therefore, they are like dreams.
The opponent says:
If all phenomena are like dreams, why is it that when an old person, a young person, or a middle-aged person takes up a jar, they do not also take up a cloth and so forth?
When one takes up a piece of cotton cloth, why does one not also take up a jar and other such things?
Now we see that one takes up a jar but does not take up other objects; because names have fixed referents, one should know that all phenomena are not like dreams.
The internal [opponent] says:
A name is not the substance itself.
If a name were the substance, then as with the name "jar," there would immediately follow the functional utility of containing milk, curd, and so forth.
As worldly wise people say: "If a jar already possesses the name 'empty,' it has served its purpose; one should not need to have a potter again fashion a jar at a mountain's price.
Likewise, the body has three names:
male, female, or neither male nor female.
If one takes the substance (body) as the basis for naming, then [all things] are subsumed under three [categories].
However, if one seeks names by means of names, then these three do not encompass one another; thus, the name and the substance are distinct.
Furthermore, just as a jar has a sound that can be heard and a color that can be seen, if its odor and tactile qualities were likewise [separately named], there would be many jars.
Furthermore, a jar has a mouth, a neck, a base, and a belly; these are called "not one," and thus there should be many jars.
Observing it in this way, one should know that names are false and lack reality.
As the Buddha said in a verse:
"The world exists as a mere designation; Its characteristics are like a mirage in the heat;
Sounds are like echoes; The characteristics of the world are like dreams."
The opponent said:
"Although you have refuted the existence of phenomena in various ways, if you say that phenomena exist, you contradict your own statement;
if you say they do not exist, what is there to be refuted?"
The internal proponent says:
If your doctrine possesses an essential nature (*svabhāva*), then I have something to refute.
If it were fundamentally without an essential nature, then I would have nothing to refute.
It is said:
"The mark of equality of the Great Man is that the mind has no defilement or attachment, nor is there any non-defilement; it abides nowhere at all."
Those who possess the characteristics of reality, who have desire or have abandoned desire,
and who have achieved indestructible faith, cast aside all false views.
Having cleared away the net of false views, all defilements are utterly extinguished.
One who can cast off the thorns of the three poisons and diligently practices the right path,
who skillfully examines such dharmas and gives rise to deep faith and reverence,
seeking the true Dharma with a faithful mind, shall not proceed toward the three realms of existence.
Not grasping at non-existence, one realizes the path of nirvāṇa;
all phenomena are not one, yet such phenomena are not different.
How could they have the mark of existence? For by their very nature, phenomena lack intrinsic substance.
It does not exist by way of having a form; inherently, this dharma is not so.
Your doctrine would thus be unestablished, as it employs no cause in this manner.
You must explain its essential nature and characteristics; otherwise, there is a fault in the claim of identity.
If that were so, there would be no substance; the five sense organs would not apprehend objects.
Though form-phenomena have names, that which is seen likewise lacks substance.
Since it exists, it need not be produced; those phenomena have no arising.
Conditioned phenomena have no intrinsic nature; even so, they possess spatial dimensions.
They are equal to dreams without distinction, and their characteristics likewise have no difference.
This is the *Śataśāstra*, spoken by Āryadeva.
The Hundred-Syllable Treatise, one fascicle.
